toyota: Toyota's catalogue is the longest continuous run of mainstream nameplates in the industry: the Corolla has been in production since 1966 and the Land Cruiser since 1951, and both still sell in volume. The pattern in the ownership record is consistency rather than brilliance — Toyota model years rarely top the complaint rankings and rarely produce a standout, with the notable exceptions of the 2007–2011 Camry and Corolla oil-consumption era and early Prius hybrid-battery age-outs. Concept cars are listed alongside production models; the FT- and FJ-prefixed entries are show cars, not catalogue variants.
ford: Ford's entries span the Model T to the current F-Series, and the United States ownership data for the marque is the deepest on the site because of sheer volume. Two nameplates dominate the complaint record: the 2011–2016 Focus and Fiesta with the PowerShift dual-clutch transmission, and the 2011–2019 Escape and Fusion with turbocharged EcoBoost engines that developed coolant-intrusion faults. Those clusters make Ford look worse in the rankings than its pickup and Mustang lines deserve. European and Australian Fords are catalogued under their regional companies.
volkswagen: Volkswagen's catalogue runs from the original Beetle and Type 2 through eight generations of Golf to the ID electric range. In the United States record the marque's complaints concentrate in two places: the 2009–2015 TDI diesels affected by the emissions scandal and the associated buy-backs, and timing-chain tensioner failures on 2008–2013 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol engines. The catalogue includes Volkswagen do Brasil and South African models that never reached Europe or North America.
bmw: BMW's library covers the Neue Klasse saloons that saved the company in the 1960s, every generation of the 3, 5 and 7 Series, the M cars and the i electric line. The ownership record shows an unusually strong split between generations: N20 and N26 four-cylinder engines (2012–2015) carry timing-chain and oil-leak complaints, while the later B-series engines are quiet. Motorsport-only cars are catalogued under BMW M and BMW Motorsport where Wikidata records them that way.
mercedes-benz: Mercedes-Benz has the longest history of any surviving marque, and this catalogue reaches back to the Benz Patent-Motorwagen. The United States ownership record for the modern range is thinner than for domestic brands because the cars sell in smaller numbers, but where the record is deep — the C-Class and E-Class of 2012 onward — the complaints are dominated by electrical and infotainment faults rather than mechanical ones. AMG models are catalogued separately where they carry their own Wikidata entry.
honda: Honda's catalogue is the largest in this library because Wikidata records its motorcycles' four-wheeled cousins, kei cars and every regional Civic and Accord derivative. The United States ownership record is one of the more instructive: the CR-V, Accord and Odyssey are large-volume nameplates with a clear generational pattern — the 2017–2019 CR-V and Civic 1.5-litre turbo oil-dilution complaints, the 2018–2020 Odyssey and Pilot nine-speed and ten-speed transmission complaints — against a long baseline of low complaint rates.
nissan: Nissan's entries include Datsun-badged export models, the Skyline and Z lineages, and the current crossover range. In the United States record the marque is defined by one component: the Jatco continuously variable transmission, which drives the complaint counts of the 2013–2018 Altima, Sentra, Rogue and Pathfinder. Model years before and after that window look markedly better, which is why the per-year verdicts on the ownership pages matter more than the nameplate's reputation.
mazda: Mazda's catalogue includes the rotary-engined Cosmo, RX-7 and RX-8, the MX-5 that reinvented the small roadster in 1989, and the current Skyactiv range. The ownership record is short on drama: complaint rates are low across most model years, with the exceptions being the 2007–2012 CX-7 turbocharged engine and rust complaints on the 2004–2009 Mazda3 and Mazda6.
audi: Audi's catalogue runs from the DKW and Auto Union ancestors through the Quattro that changed rallying to the current e-tron electric range. The United States record is shaped by the 2.0-litre TFSI engines of 2009–2013, whose oil-consumption complaints cluster on the A4, A5 and Q5, and by the wider Volkswagen Group diesel affair. Audi Sport models are catalogued separately.
hyundai: Hyundai's catalogue starts with the 1975 Pony and includes Korean-market models never sold abroad. The United States record is dominated by one engine family: the Theta II 2.0 and 2.4-litre engines in the 2011–2019 Sonata, Santa Fe and Tucson, subject to connecting-rod bearing failures, engine fires, multiple recalls and a federal consent order. Those years carry some of the highest complaint rates on the site; the later Smartstream engines do not.
kia: Kia shares platforms and engines with Hyundai, and its United States ownership record shares the same fault line: the Theta II engines in the 2011–2019 Optima, Sorento and Sportage. Kia's own catalogue also carries the Soul, the EV6 and Korean-market models. The post-2020 range has a much quieter complaint record so far.
chevrolet: Chevrolet's catalogue is General Motors' volume brand from the 1911 Series C through the Corvette, Camaro, Impala and Silverado to the Bolt EV. In the United States record two clusters stand out: the 2011–2016 Cruze and Equinox 2.4-litre oil-consumption and timing-chain complaints, and the 2017–2019 Bolt battery recall. Full-size trucks and the Corvette carry low complaint rates for their volume.
subaru: Subaru's catalogue is small and unusually consistent: nearly every model since 1972 has been a flat-four with all-wheel drive. The United States record shows two things worth knowing — head-gasket complaints on the 1999–2010 EJ25 engines, and oil-consumption complaints on the 2011–2015 FB-series engines in the Forester, Outback and Impreza — and then a generally clean record from 2016 on, apart from the Starlink infotainment.
porsche: Porsche's catalogue runs from the 356 through every generation of the 911, the front-engined 924, 944 and 928, the Boxster and Cayman, and the Cayenne, Macan and Taycan that now pay for the sports cars. The United States record is thin because the cars are low-volume, but the intermediate-shaft bearing failures of the 1997–2008 M96 and M97 engines are the single best-known fault in the marque's history and are visible in the complaint data for the 996 and early 997.
ferrari: Ferrari's catalogue is one of the most complete in this library because nearly every road and racing car the company has built has a Wikidata entry, from the 125 S of 1947 to the current hybrid range. Ownership data from the United States federal record is sparse — too few cars, too few complaints — so almost every Ferrari entry here is a catalogue page rather than a scored one.
lamborghini: Lamborghini's catalogue runs from the 350 GT and the Miura that invented the mid-engined supercar to the Countach, Diablo, Murciélago, Aventador and the Urus. The United States ownership record is too thin for verdicts; these are catalogue entries with sourced specifications where Wikipedia carries them.
jaguar: Jaguar's catalogue includes the SS100, the XK120, the E-Type, every XJ generation and the current F-Type and I-Pace. The United States record for the modern range is thin, with the 2010–2015 XF and XJ carrying the most complaints, mostly electrical.
land-rover: Land Rover's catalogue runs from the 1948 Series I through the Defender, Discovery and every Range Rover generation. The United States ownership record for the marque carries persistently high complaint rates on the 2013–2018 Range Rover and Range Rover Sport, concentrated in electrical, air-suspension and infotainment components rather than the engines.
tesla: Tesla's catalogue is short — Roadster, Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck and Semi — but the United States ownership record for it is the deepest for any electric brand, and MotorJury adds battery-warranty and replacement-cost data to every Tesla model year. The complaint pattern is distinctive: touchscreen and Autopilot complaints dominate, and the early Model S (2012–2015) carries drive-unit and door-handle complaints that later years do not.
peugeot: Peugeot's catalogue is one of the largest in the library because the company has been building cars since 1889 and Wikidata records nearly every numbered model. None are sold in the United States, so there is no ownership-cost data for the marque; these are catalogue entries with photographs and sourced specifications.
renault: Renault's catalogue reaches from the 1898 Voiturette through the 4CV, the 4, the 5 and the Espace to the current electric range, and includes the Argentinian, Korean and Renault Sport subsidiaries as separate marques. Renault has not sold cars in the United States since 1987, so the entries here are catalogue pages without federal ownership data.
fiat: Fiat's catalogue includes the 500 in every one of its incarnations, the 124 and 128 that were licensed and copied around the world, and the Brazilian and Polish derivatives. The United States ownership record covers only the 2012–2019 500, 500L and 500X, which carry high complaint rates for their volume, mostly transmission and electrical.
alfa-romeo: Alfa Romeo's catalogue runs from the 24 HP of 1910 through the Giulietta, the Giulia, the Spider and the 156 to the current Giulia and Stelvio. The United States record covers the 2017 onward Giulia and Stelvio, whose complaints concentrate in electrical and infotainment faults in the first two model years and fall sharply afterward.
jeep: Jeep's catalogue starts with the Willys MB and runs through the CJ, the Cherokee XJ, every Wrangler and Grand Cherokee generation, and the Renegade and Compass. The United States ownership record is deep and unflattering in places: the 2014–2016 Cherokee nine-speed transmission, the 2011–2013 Grand Cherokee electrical faults and the 2018–2019 Wrangler steering complaints are three of the largest clusters on the site.
dodge: Dodge's catalogue covers the Charger, Challenger, Viper, Dart, Journey and Grand Caravan, and the historic muscle-car era. In the United States record the 2013–2016 Dart and the 2011–2018 Journey carry the highest complaint rates; the modern Charger and Challenger are quiet for their volume.
lexus: Lexus's catalogue runs from the 1989 LS 400 through the IS, GS, RX and the LFA. Its United States ownership record has the lowest complaint rates of any luxury marque on the site by a wide margin; the only cluster of note is dashboard-material complaints on 2006–2010 models.
volvo: Volvo's catalogue includes the PV444, the Amazon, the 240 that defined the marque for a generation, the 850 and the current XC range. The United States record is moderate: the 2001–2009 S60 and XC90 carry transmission and electrical complaints, while the 2016 onward SPA-platform cars are quiet apart from infotainment.
mini: Mini's catalogue separates the 1959–2000 original, catalogued under British Motor Corporation and its successors, from the BMW-era cars since 2001. The United States record for the modern Mini shows a clear pattern: the 2007–2010 turbocharged Cooper S carries timing-chain and high-pressure fuel-pump complaints at rates well above later years.
lancia: Lancia's catalogue is a record of engineering firsts — the Lambda's monocoque, the Aurelia's V6, the Fulvia, the Stratos and the Delta Integrale — and of concept cars from the Bertone and Pininfarina studios. Lancia left the United States after 1982, so these are catalogue pages without federal ownership data.
citroën: Citroën's catalogue runs from the Type A of 1919 through the Traction Avant, the 2CV, the DS and the hydropneumatic era to the current range. Citroën has never sold cars in the United States in volume, so every entry here is a catalogue page.
lotus: Lotus's catalogue covers the Seven, the Elan, the Europa, the Esprit, the Elise and the current Emira and Eletre, plus the racing cars that made the company's name. The United States record is too thin for verdicts.
